title: RBI’s New Trade Regulations & Export Declaration Form (EDF) Rules: Everything Exporters and Importers Need to Know
summary: Learn what RBI’s new trade regulations mean for exporters and importers, including EDF rules, the ₹10 lakh threshold, timelines, SOFTEX changes and more.
body_markdown:
On January 13, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) notified a comprehensive new framework for exports and imports following a complete review of existing trade rules. Designed to align with evolving global trade practices and improve the ease of doing business, these principle-based regulations consolidate and supersede more than 150 earlier RBI circulars into a single reference framework.


While the regulations were issued in January 2026, they came into effect on October 01, 2026. Following the rollout, several questions have emerged around EDF rules (Export Declaration Form rule), applicability, thresholds, timelines, and documentation.


To bring further clarity, the RBI has issued official guidance addressing these questions. Below is a detailed breakdown of what the new regulations mean for Indian exporters and importers.


**Disclaimer:** The RBI FAQs are intended for general guidance only. In case of any inconsistency between the FAQs and FEMA, 1999, or the rules, regulations, directions or permissions issued under it, the latter shall prevail.


##


Scope and Applicability: Which Transactions Are Covered?


The new trade regulations govern transactions involving the export and import of goods and services, as well as merchanting trade (MTT) undertaken on or after October 01, 2026.


If a transaction (involving goods, software, or services) was initiated or undertaken prior to October 01, 2026, it is not governed by the new regulations, even if the transaction gets completed on or after October 01, 2026. Such prior transactions continue to fall under the regulatory framework that was in force when the transaction commenced. Additionally, Authorized Dealers (ADs) have now been vested with powers to grant approvals for pre-October 01, 2026 transactions, powers that were previously exercised by the RBI.


Similarly, if you exported services with an invoice date prior to October 01, 2026, and received the payment on or after October 01, 2026, you are not required to submit an EDF to the specified authority.


##


Who Needs to File an EDF for Export of Services?


One of the biggest clarifications in the RBI’s guidance concerns who actually needs to file an Export Declaration Form (EDF) and when:


- **Resident Individuals:** Resident individuals do not need to separately furnish an EDF for the export of services. For resident individuals, the EDF is deemed submitted when they provide the necessary details to their Authorised Dealer (AD), just as they did previously, for realizing the inward remittance and crediting their bank account.


- **Persons Other Than Resident Individuals (Businesses/Entities):** The EDF needs to be filed only in cases where the value of each inward remittance exceeds ₹10 lakh (or its equivalent in foreign currency).


### Releasing Inward Remittances (Other Than Export Advances)


Exporters do not need to furnish an EDF for the AD to release an inward remittance (other than an export advance) if they are:


1. A resident individual, or


2. A person other than a resident individual where the inward remittance value is up to ₹10 lakh.


Only service exporters other than resident individuals receiving an inward remittance exceeding ₹10 lakh must file the EDF before the inward remittance is credited to their account.


##


What Changed for Software Exporters (SOFTEX Discontinued)?


Starting October 01, 2026, the SOFTEX form has been discontinued for software exports.


Under the updated process, non-individual software exporters should now file the EDF instead:


- Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) exporters: File the EDF with any Authorised Dealer (AD) or the Software Technology Parks of India (STPI).
- Special Economic Zone (SEZ) exporters: The EDF may be filed with the Development Commissioner of the SEZ.


##


EDF Submission Timelines and Extensions


For non-individual service exporters where the inward remittance is more than the specified threshold, the submission timelines are as follows:


Export Scenario Deadline for EDF Submission


Export of software Within 30 days from the end of the month in which the invoice for services is raised.


Export of services other than software Within 30 days from the end of the month in which the invoice for services is raised OR on or before the date of receipt of payment.


For advance payments received for export of services, including software, the EDF needs to be submitted within 30 days from the end of the month in which the invoice for services has been raised.


##


Can the EDF Submission Deadline Be Extended?


Yes. If a service exporter cannot meet the specified timeline, the Authorised Dealer (AD) may extend the time period for submitting the EDF, provided the AD is satisfied with the reasonableness of the exporter’s request.


##


What Happens to EDF / GR Waivers?


Under the new trade regulations, the requirement for an EDF waiver (formerly known as a Guaranteed Remittance (GR) waiver) has been discontinued.


If exported goods have no realizable value, exporters simply need to declare this as zero value in the appropriate field of the EDF. Consequently, effective October 01, 2026, Authorised Dealers are no longer authorised to issue EDF or GR waiver letters.


##


How the EDF Is Structured (And What Service Exporters Fill Out)


According to the RBI, the EDF is a straightforward form divided into 5 sections:


1. General information


2. Details of export of goods or export of services


3. Information to be submitted for export of goods through Foreign Post Offices (FPO) and Couriers


4. Declaration by the exporter


5. Certification by the authorised person having received the EDF


What applies to service exports: For the export of services, the only sections required are general information, details of export of service, and the declaration by the exporter. Furthermore, the section covering


*details of export of services* needs to be filled out only by persons other than resident individuals when the inward remittance exceeds ₹10 lakh (or its equivalent in foreign currency).


##


Rules for Import of Services


For resident individuals, and for businesses whose invoice or contract value is up to ₹10 lakh, the process for importing services remains unchanged under the new regime:


- Prior to October 01, 2026, Authorised Dealers permitted outward remittances for service imports after collecting necessary information from the importer to verify the bona fides of the transaction.
- Under the new regulations, the same approach continues for resident individuals and persons other than resident individuals whose invoice or contract value is up to ₹10 lakh. Providing the standard information sought by your AD for outward remittances continues to suffice.


##


E/IDPMS Reporting, Voluntary Filings, and Reconciliation Rules


### 1. Reporting by Authorised Dealers in E/IDPMS


Even when resident individuals or non-individual entities fall within the up to ₹10 lakh threshold, Authorised Dealers are still required to report the transaction details (specifically the Inward Remittance Message and Outward Remittance Message, as applicable) in the Export/Import Data Processing and Monitoring System (E/IDPMS).


### 2. Voluntary Submission of EDF or Import Invoices


If an exporter or importer of services (whether a resident individual or a non-individual entity) voluntarily submits an EDF or import invoice even when not mandated, the Authorised Dealer may record those details in the E/IDPMS system and subsequently reconcile them with the corresponding remittance messages.


### 3. Eligibility for Simplified E/IDPMS Reconciliation


The simplified reconciliation process in E/IDPMS for bills up to ₹10 lakh applies strictly to transactions where the total shipping bill/bill of entry value (for goods) or invoice value (for services) is up to ₹10 lakh (or its foreign currency equivalent).


You


**cannot** use the simplified reconciliation process if the overall bill or invoice value exceeds ₹10 lakh, even if the remaining outstanding balance is ₹10 lakh or less.


##


How to Check Your Bank’s Specific Trade SOPs


With the new framework delegating broader authority to Authorised Dealers to handle foreign trade transactions, customers can review how their specific bank processes these transactions. Under Regulation 19(4) of the new Trade Regulations, every Authorised Dealer is mandated to publish its trade-related policy and the main features of its Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for handling trade transactions directly on its website.


*For full regulatory text, stakeholders can refer to the official notification and FAQ portal on the


[Reserve Bank of India website](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/FAQView.aspx?Id=181) .
